newsitem.title: USA: N.J. treasurer eyes May for $3 bln bond sale--RFTV.
newsitem.headline: N.J. treasurer eyes May for $3 bln bond sale--RFTV.

text.p: New Jersey Treasurer Brian Clymer said the state hopes to sell its proposed $2.9 billion pension bond deal in May, assuming the state Legislature approves the issue in the next 30 days.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television to be aired Thursday, Clymer said he hoped lawmakers would act promptly on the measure to take advantage of current low market rates.
"In the perfect world we'd like to see it addressed by the Legislature within the next 30 days, and then probably in the next month or so after that we'd see the bonds go to market," Clymer said."
The Treasurer, Gov. Christine Whitman's point man in generating support for the issue, also defended the idea against a wide range of attacks from opponents in the state.

The key reasons for selling what would be the largest single bond issue in municipal market history include the elimination of the system's $4.2 billion unfunded liability and the long-term savings to the pension system, Clymer said.
The deal would restructure $57 billion of state debt over 60 years into a 35-year debt totaling $15 billion, saving $42 billion, he said.
The plan also envisions using $1.3 billion of a pension fund surplus, a portion of which would free up about $650 million in one-shot budget savings for the administration.

Critics of the idea argue that it eliminates flexibility, since the pension system payments are relatively malleable in the amounts the state must contribute each year. A bond sale, on the other hand, creates a fixed, unchangeable debt service schedule.

But Clymer said the state is not giving up flexibility in the exchange. "That presupposes that the commitment that we've made to our employees to pay this liability is one that we would take away in the future, and I don't think that's the case."
Clymer said if the pension system continues to earn above expectations, the formula allows the state to offset future payments into the system.
The governor's Democratic opponents in the state Legislature have been lobbying for a public referendum, taking note of opinion polls which show deep skepticism about the bond issue.
But Clymer said in the interview that a vote on the bonds would not be necessary, since the policy decision on spending the money had already been decided.

"I think this is a case where the horse is already out of the barn," Clymer said. "These benefits were granted a decade ago, and if you were going to vote on the purpose of the bond issue, the purpose was really something established by the Legislature when they conferred these benefits on our retirees probably 10 years ago.

"The other problem is if I wait nine months, I could end up losing the market and rendering the whole deal moot," Clymer added. "I have the opportunity to lock in substantial savings for taxpayers right now and I think it's our obligation to do that."

The Treasurer said the major credit rating agencies believe the deal is "credit neutral," since it replaces one obligation with another. But they have expressed concern about the use of $650 million in one-shot revenues generated by the deal.
Clymer said the one-shot is lower than in previous budgets, showing that New Jersey "is actually in a stronger financial position today than it was last year or the year before."

He also said it makes sense to tap the pension system's surplus to save money for the state. "We have a surplus that currently exists of almost $3.6 billion. It just doesn't make sense to put taxpayer dollars -- about $300 million this year and $300 million next year -- into a pension system that has such a huge surplus."
After the deal is completed the remaining surplus would be $1.7 billion, "which we think is a prudent level to protect against future market fluctuations," Clymer said.

The Treasurer also denied that the success of the bond deal relies on continued strong performance by the stock market. "We don't rely on continued very strong growth in the market," Clymer said, noting that the deal envisions an 8-3/4 percent annual return on investments.
Two years ago, in contrast, the state earned over 28 percent, and it made 16 percent last year, he said.
Over the past 70 years, the state has averaged 9.3 percent percent, and 12 percent over the last decade, Clymer said.
"Our expectations of 8-3/4 percent are prudent, they're reasonable, they're achievable and history has shown that we can do that."
